# Hard-to-vary reading of *The Time Machine*, chs. I–VI (excerpt)

## 1. The question, frozen

The document answers several things at once (why the Eloi are frail; why the future is dilapidated), but the excerpt's opening and its title make one thing central: **what makes the claim "a machine can carry a person through time" hold together for the listeners** — the Time Traveller's Fourth-Dimension argument, his tabletop demonstration, and his own battered return, all offered as one connected case for "this is real, not a trick." Range: from the dinner-table debate through the vanishing model to his account of the outward journey and landing, stopping where the supplied text stops (mid-Chapter V/VI, before the Eloi/Morlock explanation, which is not in front of me and is not tested here). Kind of question: mainly "what produces it?" (what makes travel-through-time physically possible), with a "can we trust what we saw?" strand running alongside.

## 2. The explanation in parts

- **A.** Time is a fourth dimension, structurally like the other three; only our consciousness moves along it, one way, one speed.
- **B.** An "instantaneous cube" cannot exist, so any real thing must have extension in time as well as space — offered as the ground for A.
- **C.** The balloon-and-gravity analogy: a device could let a person move against time's normal drift, as a balloon lets one move against gravity.
- **D.** The demonstration: the model vanishes before several witnesses seated all round it, with a breath of wind and a blown-out candle, staged so no simple trick could explain it.
- **E.** The Psychologist's "presentation below the threshold" — an object moving fast through time would be too dim/brief to see, patching the objection "if it went to the past, we'd have seen it here all along."
- **F.** The stated danger of stopping: jamming your atoms into whatever already occupies that space, with a possible explosion — set up as the risk that makes the journey perilous.
- **G.** The physical evidence on return: dirt, a half-healed cut, blood-stained socks, a limp, ravenous hunger.

## 3. Part by part

| Part | Mark | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A (time = 4th dimension) | **Held if** | Held only by the job "the vanishing has no rival explanation" — a job the scene itself puts in doubt (the Medical Man and Psychologist both float "trick"). Swap A for "some other force removes things from the present" and the witnessed event looks identical. |
| B (instantaneous cube) | **Loose** | A different warm-up analogy (a photograph as a flat slice of a solid person) would do the same persuading with no change to anything that follows. What's actually held, if anything, is the more general "duration is a dimension," not this specific cube. |
| C (balloon analogy) | **Idle** | Remove it and the demonstration, the journey, the return are all untouched. It is scaffolding for the listeners' (and reader's) comfort, not a working part of any event in the story. |
| D (the vanishing demonstration) | **Held** | By the job "rule out an easy stage-trick." The specific staging — witnesses on every side, room brightly lit, a search under the table — is there because a weaker staging (one witness, dim room, no search) would fail that job. This is the part the rest of Chapter III's suspense actually depends on. |
| E (threshold patch) | **Loose, ungauged catch-all** | It appears exactly when a contradiction threatens (why wasn't the machine visible here all along, if it went to the past?) and is accepted with no test proposed ("Of course," said the Psychologist). Swap the jargon for any other invented term and the scene is unchanged — the label does no work, only its presence does. The method calls for a gauge on any catch-all; none is given. |
| F (collision-on-stopping risk) | **Idle**, as an explanation of what's actually shown | It is built up as the reason a return would be dangerous, but the injuries we actually see (a cut chin, dirt, blood-stained socks) come from ordinary causes in the text itself — the machine physically overturning, hail, days of walking — not from matter-jamming. The dramatic hazard is never the thing that does the explaining; it raises stakes and is then quietly dropped. |
| G (bodily evidence on return) | **Held** | By the job "make faking this look too costly to be worth it." Swap "blood-stained socks and a limp" for "a slightly wrinkled suit" and the job fails — a wrinkled suit is cheap to fake and wouldn't dent the room's mockery the way visible wounds do. Note also that only the narrator notices the limp at first; the evidence has to be *seen* to do its job, and the text is careful to route it through one witness before others catch up. |

## 4. Whole-explanation checks

**Flip.** An unmarked return with the same story would not have moved the room from mockery to unease, so that arc genuinely rests on G, not on A–C.

**Pairs that pull.** A–C aim at credibility through argument; D and G aim at it through checkable, sensory fact. The text shows which wins: Filby sits through the whole geometry lecture unmoved ("you will never convince me"), while the room goes quiet only once wounds appear. Argument buys less belief here than one bleeding foot.

**Rival explanation.** Drop the Fourth-Dimension argument for a bare "he built a machine, don't ask how" — does the listeners' behavior change? No: their swing from mockery to unease tracks the demonstration and the wounds, not the geometry. At the level of *what makes the room believe him*, the two are the same explanation. The geometry's real job is external — giving a reader of "scientific romance" the genre's expected veneer — a job the in-story list can't test. Call it **borrowed** from the genre, not held by anything in the scene.

**Gaps.** The excerpt ends before the Eloi's decline is explained; the sphinx, ruins and fruit diet are set-ups for a part not supplied, so they are **unknown** here, not tested.

## 5. What would tighten it most

Give F an actual job: have the return's injuries trace to a near-miss of the stated collision risk, not an unrelated tumble. Give E a gauge: some in-story test (someone tries to touch the blurring machine and fails in a specific, checkable way) rather than taking the Psychologist's word for it.

## 6. What this does not show

Hard to vary is not truth. None of this bears on whether time travel is possible, whether Wells's Victorian physics is sound, or whether the passage is good writing — only on which of its own stated parts are actually doing the work of persuading the room, and which are asserted decoration.

## 7. One next step

Read the excised scientific-romance framing (A–C) against the by-domain "arguments" test specifically — hunt the answer in the starting points — to see whether "time is a fourth dimension" is doing independent work anywhere later in the novel, or whether it is used once here and never called on again.
